 I Drove 442 Miles to Vote. As a Law Student, I Knew Not to Take No for an Answer. 
 Kennedy Wright | Mercer University School of Law | US 
 November 12, 2026 01:34:24 pm 
Edited by:
 Ingrid Burke Friedman | JURIST Editorial Director Told at the polls that she couldn’t vote because of an unreturned absentee ballot, a law student knew to ask for a provisional ballot. She argues every voter should know that option exists. 442 miles.
 That is how far I drove round trip in a single day to exercise my right to vote in the 2026 midterm election.
 I traveled from Macon, Georgia, to Greenville, South Carolina, determined to make my voice heard.
 What I expected to be a straightforward trip home became an experience that reminded me of why voting matters, why understanding our rights is so important, and why I remain hopeful about the future of our democracy.
 In the weeks leading up to Election Day, I found myself reflecting on an open letter published by my law professor, Gary Simson, in JURIST, titled “ Students, Your Freedoms Are on the Line. Here’s How to Defend Them .” His letter warned that the current administration poses a serious threat to constitutional freedoms, the rule of law, and democratic institutions. Professor Simson urged college and law students to take an active role in defending those principles by voting, holding government officials accountable, and speaking out against government overreach rather than remaining silent or becoming complacent. His message was a reminder that our education comes with an obligation to do more than simply understand the law. We must be willing to use what we learn to make a difference.
 I did not anticipate how personally meaningful that message would become on Election Day.
 I had every intention of voting by mail. I submitted an application for an absentee ballot in July and regularly checked its status throughout the summer. When I still had not received any updates, I contacted my local election office in September. That was when I discovered that my application had never been received. Somewhere along the way, it had been lost.
 The election office mailed me an entirely new application, which I submitted before the deadline. Unfortunately, my actual mail-in ballot was also delayed, and I did not receive it until the Friday before Election Day. With so little time remaining and no guarantee that my completed ballot would make it back in time, I made the decision to drive home to Greenville and vote in person.
 I was determined to make my voice heard. I just did not realize how much determination it would take.
 Fortunately, I learned about provisional ballots weeks before Election Day. During a voter education event hosted by Mercer Votes and the Mercer Law Black Law Students Association, I learned about the role provisional ballots play in protecting election participation. Although completing a provisional ballot does not guarantee that it will be counted, it provides an important mechanism for ensuring that if a voter’s eligibility is called into question, the matter will be addressed with the care it deserves and not simply treated as an automatic disqualification. The discussion prompted me to do additional research into South Carolina’s provisional ballot procedures so I would understand my options before arriving at the polls.
 When I arrived at my polling location, I was initially told that I could not vote because an absentee ballot had already been issued in my name. I explained that I had the ballot with me, had not returned it, and wanted to vote in person instead. The poll worker insisted that I was not permitted to do so because of the outstanding absentee ballot.
 Because of what I had learned and the research I had done, I knew there was another option. I requested a provisional ballot and asked to speak with a supervisor. I knew that holding an absentee ballot did not mean that I had surrendered my opportunity to vote. But I also recognized that knowing I had another option and successfully navigating the process were two different things. After speaking with approximately three additional poll workers, I was finally permitted to complete a provisional ballot.
 In that moment, I was reminded of something I have spent much of my legal education learning: knowing your rights matters. Had I not attended that voter education event or researched South Carolina’s procedures, I might have accepted the first answer, turned around, and left. Instead, I was able to advocate for myself and rely on my understanding of the voting process to find a way forward. I left my polling location feeling proud, grateful, and empowered that I had exercised my right to vote despite the obstacles.
 The information I received at a campus event in Macon, Georgia, ultimately helped me navigate a voting issue hundreds of miles away in Greenville, South Carolina. That is the power of sharing knowledge. My experience reinforced the importance of ensuring that people understand not only that they have rights, but also how to exercise them. Provisional ballots, for example, are an important safeguard in our election system, but that safeguard is only meaningful if voters know it exists and understand how to access it. This is why voter education, community engagement, and accessible information are so important. The more we understand our rights, the better equipped we are to exercise them and help others do the same.
 The day became even more special because I also had the opportunity to encourage my younger brother to vote. This was his first election, and he was understandably intimidated by the process and some of the interactions with poll workers. I was able to stand beside him and remind him that he had every right to be there.
 There is something incredibly significant about witnessing someone exercise a right for the very first time. I remember how important that first opportunity to vote felt to me, and I wanted my brother to have an equally meaningful experience. I wanted him to understand that his voice mattered just as much as anyone else’s and that he should never feel discouraged from participating in a process that belongs to him, too. I was also reminded that civic engagement is contagious. When we encourage one another to participate, share what we know, and stand beside those who may feel uncertain, we strengthen not only individual voices but our communities as a whole.
 I am incredibly proud of the American people for showing up at the polls this November. It was a historic election, and I left the experience feeling more hopeful about our country than I had in a long time. I recognize that one election does not resolve every challenge facing our democracy. There is still work to be done to ensure that opportunity, representation, and justice are realities for everyone. But I am encouraged by the people who showed up, the conversations that were sparked, and the collective recognition that our voices have the power to shape the future. I believe there is tremendous potential in this country, and I remain hopeful that we are moving toward a future that reflects the very best of what America can be: a country where everyone’s voice matters and where opportunity is not limited by circumstance.
 For me, that hope is closely connected to the responsibility I feel as a law student and future attorney. In his JURIST open letter, Professor Simson challenged students to consider how we should respond to the threats facing democracy and the rule of law. I believe one answer begins with recognizing that our legal education is not simply a personal accomplishment. It is an opportunity to equip ourselves with the knowledge and skills to serve others.
 As future attorneys, we have an obligation to advocate, to speak up when something is wrong, and to help ensure that people have the opportunity to make their voices heard. We can do that in courtrooms, in our communities, through public service, and sometimes in the simplest of ways: by sharing information, encouraging someone to vote, or reminding another person that they have every right to stand up for themselves. Legal knowledge should not be confined to courtrooms, law offices, or academic discussions. It should be shared in our communities and made accessible to the people whose lives it affects.
 I drove 442 miles to cast one ballot. I left Greenville believing that our collective voices can make a difference. The future of our democracy is not something we should approach with resignation or fear. It is something we have the opportunity, and the responsibility, to shape. I hope we continue showing up for one another, encouraging one another, and refusing to take for granted the rights that allow us to participate in our democracy. An informed voice is an empowered voice, and democracy is strengthened every time someone chooses to participate, every time someone stands up for their rights, and every time we remind one another that our voices matter.
 Kennedy Wright is a third-year law student at Mercer University School of Law in Macon, Georgia.
